stories.headline: Update: Homicide Convictions Reversed for Paramedics in Elijah McClain Ketamine Death; New Trials Ordered
stories.summary:
A Colorado appeals court on Thursday reversed criminally negligent homicide convictions against two Aurora Fire Rescue paramedics, Jeremy Cooper and Peter Cichuniec, in the 2019 death of Elijah McClain. The court found fault with jury instructions used during the 2023 trial and ordered new trials on the homicide charges, while upholding Cichuniec's second-degree assault conviction. Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser announced his office would appeal the ruling, calling the original prosecutions "the right thing to do for justice."

McClain, a 23-year-old Black massage therapist, died after police stopped him in the Denver suburb of Aurora in response to a suspicious person complaint, placed him in a neck hold, and called paramedics who injected him with an overdose of ketamine. His final words — "I can't breathe" — became part of the social justice rallying cries that swept the U.S. following George Floyd's death in 2020. A separate Aurora police officer was previously convicted of homicide in the case; two other officers were acquitted.

The case drew national attention partly because criminal prosecution of paramedics in police custody deaths is rare. Legal experts said Thursday's ruling and the prospect of new trials could reverberate through emergency medical services nationwide, potentially influencing how first responders behave when treating individuals in police custody. University of Miami criminologist Alex Piquero noted the case would remain in the back of responders' minds during future calls.

Cichuniec, who had received a five-year prison sentence later reduced to probation, and Cooper, who had avoided prison with jail time and work release, will face new proceedings on the homicide charge. The appeals court's decision leaves the assault conviction against Cichuniec intact.

stories.headline: Update: Trump's Name Must Be Removed From Kennedy Center by June 12 Under Court-Ordered Memo
stories.summary:
The Kennedy Center's general counsel issued a memo Thursday directing all staff to remove President Trump's name from the building's signage, website, email signatures, letterhead and documents by June 12, following a federal court ruling that the board had exceeded its authority in rebranding the facility. The directive follows a May 29 ruling by U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who found the board's unanimous December vote to add Trump's name was legally improper and gave the center 14 days to undo the change.

The Kennedy Center said in a statement it was complying with the court order "while evaluating all legal options to preserve this revitalization and recognize President Trump's leadership." The broader May 29 ruling also found that the board's vote to close the center for two years of renovations was "ill-informed" and directed that future closure decisions be made in closer consultation with the full board. Trump subsequently said he was backing away from the renovation plans and would return congressional oversight of the center.

The December renaming drew immediate backlash from the Kennedy family. Kerry Kennedy wrote on social media that President Kennedy "proudly stood for justice, peace, equality, dignity, diversity, and compassion," and that Trump's name should not be placed alongside his. The center remains one of several Washington landmarks Trump has sought to rename or physically alter as part of his agenda tied to the country's 250th anniversary.

The court order represents a concrete legal setback for the administration's effort to reshape national cultural institutions. The Kennedy Center said it is still weighing options regarding the planned renovations, with the memo noting the center is "considering its options" on potential future closure.

stories.headline: Update: Ukrainian Drones Strike St. Petersburg Suburbs and Naval Base as Putin's Economic Forum Opens
stories.summary:
Ukraine launched a large-scale drone attack on Russia's second-largest city on Thursday, striking multiple districts in St. Petersburg and the nearby naval town of Kronstadt hours before President Vladimir Putin was set to address the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum. Russian authorities said air defenses shot down 59 drones overnight, but acknowledged strikes across three districts. Thick black smoke was visible over the city's waterfront, and St. Petersburg's Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed. Mobile internet was also disrupted across the region, and air raid alerts were issued in parts of Latvia and Estonia.

President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Ukrainian forces struck an oil terminal and a naval base at Kronstadt, home to the Russian Navy's Baltic Fleet. Ukrainian drone commander Robert Brovdi said the corvette Boikiy was hit, though this could not be independently verified. Zelensky described the strikes as part of Ukraine's "long-range sanctions" strategy aimed at degrading Russian military and energy infrastructure.

The timing was deliberately provocative. The St. Petersburg Economic Forum — once dubbed the "Russian Davos" — attracted thousands of guests from 130 countries, including, for the first time in nearly a decade, a low-key U.S. delegation led by the head of the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov warned that Moscow's response "will be systemic in nature." No fatalities from Thursday's strike were reported by Russian authorities.

The attack marks a further escalation in Ukraine's long-range strike campaign inside Russian territory. In recent days, Ukrainian drones have also hit a St. Petersburg oil terminal and a passenger bus in Russian-controlled territory, killing seven. Ukraine has significantly expanded its drone capabilities since Russia's 2022 invasion and increasingly targets energy infrastructure it argues fuels the Russian war machine.

stories.headline: DOJ Opens Civil Rights Investigations Into 15 More Medical Schools Over Race-Based Admissions
stories.summary:
The Department of Justice announced Thursday it has opened civil rights investigations into 15 additional U.S. medical schools over allegations of illegal race-conscious admissions practices. The DOJ's Civil Rights Division said it will examine whether the schools, each of which receives millions in federal funding, are in compliance with federal anti-discrimination law. The announcement follows recent DOJ findings that medical schools at UCLA and Yale illegally used race as a factor in admissions decisions.

The department did not publicly identify the 15 schools under investigation or provide specific evidence of wrongdoing, saying the investigations were opened to ensure federal compliance. Earlier probes at Ohio State University and Stanford University were also cited as precedents for the expanded effort. The action is part of the Trump administration's broader campaign against diversity, equity, and inclusion programs in higher education.

Supporters of the initiative argue that race-conscious admissions violate the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, which prohibited considering race in college admissions. Critics, including civil rights advocates and many medical educators, counter that diversity in medical education improves health outcomes for underserved communities and that the administration is using the investigations to intimidate institutions and dismantle diversity programs through regulatory pressure rather than litigation.

The expansion of DOJ scrutiny to medical schools signals that the administration is moving beyond undergraduate admissions enforcement into professional and graduate education. Medical schools have argued that diverse physician workforces are a matter of public health, while opponents contend that admissions must be race-neutral under current law regardless of the downstream rationale.

stories.headline: House Oversight Releases Bondi Transcript on Epstein Files; Ex-AG Points Finger at Acting AG Blanche
stories.summary:
The House Oversight and Government Reform Committee released Thursday the transcript of its closed-door interview with former Attorney General Pam Bondi concerning her handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files. The roughly four-hour session produced significant gaps in the record: Bondi declined to answer a number of questions and repeatedly attributed responsibility for overseeing the Epstein file review to Todd Blanche, who served as acting attorney general. The committee also released the transcript of an interview with a prison guard who was on duty the night Epstein died.

Bondi left the Justice Department earlier this year and her testimony before the Oversight Committee was among the first formal congressional attempts to obtain answers about why the much-anticipated Epstein files have not been fully released to the public. The disclosures have become a politically charged issue, with members of both parties pressing for transparency on the matter.

The release of the transcripts marks a new development in the committee's investigation, providing the public its first detailed look at what Bondi said — and declined to say — under questioning. The finger-pointing toward Blanche complicates the accountability chain at the Justice Department and is likely to intensify congressional scrutiny of how the Epstein materials have been managed under the current administration.

The Epstein files have remained a persistent bipartisan flashpoint since Trump's return to office, with many supporters of the president having expected a full public release of documents related to Epstein's associates. The committee's investigation is ongoing, and further hearings or document requests are expected.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Bolsters SEC's Power to Recover Illegal Profits
stories.summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday issued a ruling reinforcing the Securities and Exchange Commission's authority to recoup illegal gains from wrongdoers, reaffirming one of the agency's most significant enforcement tools. The decision strengthens the SEC's hand in cases where it seeks disgorgement — the return of profits derived from fraudulent or unlawful activity — following years of legal challenges that had placed limits on the practice.

The ruling is a notable win for financial regulators at a moment when the SEC's enforcement posture has been closely watched. Prior Supreme Court decisions had narrowed disgorgement authority, and Wednesday's ruling pushes back against that trend by giving the agency broader latitude to pursue ill-gotten gains.

The case is expected to have wide practical implications for securities enforcement, particularly in complex fraud cases where defendants have argued that disgorgement amounts exceeded what courts could lawfully order. Plaintiffs' attorneys and investor advocates are likely to view the decision as a meaningful expansion of investor protections.

The ruling arrives amid broader scrutiny of federal regulatory power across multiple agencies, making it a significant data point in ongoing legal debates about the scope of administrative enforcement authority.

stories.headline: Dutch Police Arrest Four Men in Investigation Into Drugging and Sexual Assault of Multiple Women
stories.summary:
Dutch national police announced Thursday that four men have been arrested following an investigation into the suspected drugging and sexual assault of an unknown number of women in the Netherlands. Authorities said the suspects allegedly operated within private social media groups where tips on how to drug victims were shared and images of the alleged abuse were circulated, with the investigation triggered by tip-offs from agencies in England and Germany.

Police raided the homes of eight suspects — men aged 21 to 51 — in late May, seizing computers, phones, USB sticks, SD cards, drugs, and weapons from several locations. Charges against those arrested vary and include participation in the online groups, creation or distribution of sexual imagery, and endangering victims through drugging "up to and including (attempted) rape."

The full scope of the alleged abuse remains unclear, as investigators are still determining how many women may have been victimized. Authorities noted that victims may be unaware they were targeted because they were unconscious after being drugged. "This is a case with an enormous impact," said Milou van der Kolk of the Rotterdam sexual crimes team.

Dutch media have drawn comparisons to the high-profile case of Gisèle Pelicot in France, in which a husband repeatedly drugged his wife and invited men to assault her — a trial that drew widespread international attention to the phenomenon of drug-facilitated sexual assault. Police said further arrests are possible as the investigation continues.

stories.headline: Persepolis Author Marjane Satrapi Dies at 56
stories.summary:
Marjane Satrapi, the French-Iranian author, illustrator, filmmaker, and activist best known for her graphic novel series and animated film Persepolis, died Thursday at age 56. France's Élysée Palace confirmed her death, with President Emmanuel Macron paying tribute to "a great artist who transformed an Iranian childhood into a universal fable." A member of her inner circle told AFP she had "died of sadness" more than a year after the death of her husband, Mattias Ripa.

Satrapi's Persepolis, first published in 2000, chronicled her childhood in Tehran during and after the 1979 Iranian Revolution and her subsequent exile in Europe. The animated film adaptation, which she co-directed, was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature in 2008 and starred Chiara Mastroianni and Catherine Deneuve. The work became a landmark of both graphic literature and international cinema, translated into dozens of languages.

An outspoken critic of Iran's government throughout her life, Satrapi said her purpose with Persepolis was to humanize Iranian people for Western audiences. She became a French citizen in 2006, though last year she declined France's Legion d'honneur, citing what she described as her adopted country's "hypocrisy" in its dealings with Iran.

Tributes poured in from French cultural and political figures. National Assembly President Yaël Braun-Pivet said France had lost "an immense artist" who had "turned her work into an act of freedom" and given "a face and a voice to the Iranian revolution."

stories.headline: North Korea Unveils New Plant to Produce Weapons-Grade Uranium
stories.summary:
North Korea has revealed a new facility designed to produce highly enriched uranium for nuclear weapons, with state media photographs indicating the plant is intended for weapons-grade fuel production. Leader Kim Jong Un described the expansion as necessary in response to worsening security threats and what he characterized as long-term confrontations with the country's 'most ferocious enemies,' understood to refer primarily to the United States and South Korea.

The disclosure represents a concrete step in North Korea's ongoing effort to expand its nuclear arsenal and delivery capabilities. Weapons-grade uranium enrichment allows for the production of more compact and versatile nuclear warheads compared to plutonium-based designs, and a new dedicated facility signals a scaling up of industrial-level production capacity.

The announcement comes amid already heightened regional tensions and an ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict that has preoccupied American military and diplomatic attention. Analysts have previously warned that periods of U.S. distraction in the Middle East create windows for North Korea to accelerate its weapons programs with reduced international scrutiny.

No immediate response from the United States, South Korea, or Japan was reported. The revelation is likely to intensify calls for renewed international pressure on Pyongyang, though multilateral sanctions enforcement has grown increasingly difficult given North Korea's deepened ties with Russia and China.

stories.headline: Charges Dropped Against Budapest Mayor Over 2025 Pride March After EU Court Ruling
stories.summary:
Hungarian prosecutors dropped charges against Budapest Mayor Gergely Karacsony on Thursday over his role in organizing the city's 2025 Pride march, which went ahead despite a national law banning public LGBTQ events. Prosecutors cited a landmark April ruling by the European Court of Justice, which found that Hungary's anti-LGBTQ laws violate EU rules and infringe on the bloc's values of equality and minority rights.

Karacsony had been charged in January after the June 2025 march drew a record 200,000 participants. The mayor had defiantly declared at the event that 'neither freedom nor love can be banned in Budapest,' directly challenging then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán's government. The law in question had banned so-called promotion of homosexuality or gender change to minors, framed by the government as child protection legislation.

The dismissal of charges comes just days after Hungarians voted to end Orbán's 16-year continuous rule, with Péter Magyar subsequently sworn in as the country's new prime minister. The convergence of the ECJ ruling, the political transition, and the dropped charges represents a significant shift in Hungary's legal and political landscape on LGBTQ rights.

The case had been closely watched across Europe as a test of whether EU member states could use domestic law to override EU fundamental rights protections. The ECJ's April ruling, now cited directly by Hungarian prosecutors, affirmed the primacy of EU law and set a precedent with implications for similar legislation in other member states.

stories.headline: Obama Presidential Center Opens Preview to Public Ahead of Juneteenth Launch
stories.summary:
The Obama Presidential Center in Chicago has opened for preview visits to tens of thousands of guests — including students, journalists, and staff families — ahead of its formal public opening on Juneteenth. The nearly $850 million campus on Chicago's South Side covers roughly 20 acres and is designed to reflect both the political legacy and personal values of Barack Obama, the nation's first Black president.

The museum tower houses an admission-based exhibition that is the first fully digital presidential museum, with no original documents on display. Its centerpiece is a life-sized replica of the Oval Office where visitors can sit behind the president's desk. Other exhibits span Obama's two presidential campaigns, key policy moments, and White House life, while Michelle Obama's iconic ball gowns are also on display.

Beyond the museum, the campus includes a new Chicago Public Library branch, a basketball court, and a public picnic area with grills — amenities Obama specifically requested to make the center a community gathering space on the South Side. The project is expected to draw up to one million visitors annually and is anticipated to generate significant economic activity for the surrounding neighborhood.

The Obama Foundation described the center as 'a safe space for people to come and reflect on the historic moments of this presidency' while also serving as a platform for civic engagement. The opening on Juneteenth — a federal holiday commemorating the end of slavery — was a deliberate choice reflecting the significance of Obama's historic presidency.

stories.headline: Update: California Governor's Race Still Undecided as Ballot Counting Continues; House Passes Iran War Powers Resolution
stories.summary:
California's gubernatorial primary remains unresolved days after Tuesday's voting, with conservative pundit Steve Hilton narrowly leading the crowded field, followed by former Health and Human Services Secretary Xavier Becerra and investor Tom Steyer. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass has advanced to a November runoff in her bid for a second term, though her opponent remains undetermined, with former reality TV personality Spencer Pratt a potential finalist. The ballot-counting process could take days or weeks under California's rules.

In a significant development on Capitol Hill, the House passed a war powers resolution Wednesday directing an end to U.S. military engagement in Iran, with four Republicans — Tom Barrett, Warren Davidson, Brian Fitzpatrick, and Thomas Massie — joining Democrats in a rare bipartisan rebuke of President Trump. The measure still faces a Senate vote and does not immediately halt military operations. Speaker Mike Johnson said he spent three hours at the White House with Trump, Vance, and Rubio discussing what Trump called "the final piece" needed to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump confirmed Wednesday that he sharply criticized Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over Lebanon during a tense call, telling the New York Post's Miranda Devine that he did call Netanyahu "fucking crazy" and threatened him with prison. The admission underscores a widening rift between the two leaders over Lebanon and the Iran conflict. Meanwhile, House Democrats and Republicans clashed over Rep. Rashida Tlaib's Lebanon war powers resolution, with Republican Rep. Max Miller accusing Tlaib of ties to Hezbollah on the House floor.

The Senate, separately, was launching a voting marathon on a $70 billion immigration enforcement package, after earlier delays caused by the now-abandoned "anti-weaponization fund." Republicans framed the bill as essential border security funding; Democrats argued it lacked oversight provisions and objected to several riders. The legislative week also brought fresh controversy over Trump's appointment of Bill Pulte as acting director of national intelligence, with Democrats threatening to allow warrantless surveillance authorities to lapse unless the nomination is withdrawn.

stories.headline: Iran Permits UN Nuclear Inspection at Bushehr but Stonewalls on Uranium Stockpile
stories.summary:
Iran allowed International Atomic Energy Agency monitors to visit its Bushehr nuclear power plants this week, offering a limited gesture of transparency even as it refused to cooperate with inspectors seeking to verify the condition and location of its enriched uranium stockpile. The partial access comes amid ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict and fragile diplomatic efforts to reach a nuclear deal.

The distinction between what Iran permitted and what it blocked is significant: Bushehr is a civilian power-generation facility, while the enriched uranium stockpile is the central proliferation concern for Western governments and international inspectors. Iran's refusal to account for its uranium holdings directly undermines verification efforts that any credible nuclear agreement would require.

President Trump said Wednesday that a deal with Iran could be finalized as soon as this weekend, with the White House describing a prospective agreement as one that would permanently block Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Iran, however, said there had been no progress in talks following recent tit-for-tat strikes. The mixed signals reflect the volatile and uncertain state of diplomacy between Washington and Tehran.

The IAEA inspection development adds a new concrete dimension to the ongoing standoff, illustrating the gap between the two sides on verification — historically the most contentious issue in nuclear negotiations with Iran. Any deal that does not resolve the question of the existing uranium stockpile would face significant skepticism from nonproliferation experts and U.S. lawmakers.

stories.headline: Israeli Strikes Kill 11 in Gaza City, Including Children, Despite Ceasefire
stories.summary:
Israeli aircraft struck at least four residential buildings in Gaza City in the early hours of Thursday, killing at least 11 Palestinians including women and children and wounding dozens more, according to medical sources and eyewitnesses. The strikes hit the Sheikh Radwan and Tel al-Hawa neighborhoods and the Shati refugee camp, with witnesses describing simultaneous explosions from helicopters hovering over the coastline.

Among those killed was a Hamas commander in northern Gaza, Hassan Labad, along with his wife, three of their children — two of whom had disabilities — and three other women, according to Hamas's Civil Defence agency. Israel has not commented on the strikes. Israel has continued military operations in Gaza since a U.S.-brokered ceasefire took effect last October, citing Hamas's continued rearming and rebuilding of forces.

More than 940 people have been killed in Gaza since that ceasefire, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, which also reports more than 72,950 total deaths since the conflict began following Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack on southern Israel that killed approximately 1,200 Israelis and took 251 hostage. Israel has announced plans to expand the area of Gaza under its control to 70%, raising further alarm among humanitarian organizations.

The continued strikes underscore the fragility of the ceasefire and the deteriorating humanitarian situation in Gaza, even as international attention remains heavily focused on the U.S.-Iran conflict and Lebanon. The international community has repeatedly called for a permanent halt to hostilities and increased humanitarian access to the territory.

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Strikes Crimea, Killing Four; Drone Hits Commuter Train as Attacks Widen
stories.summary:
Russian-installed authorities in occupied Crimea reported at least four people killed in Ukrainian strikes on Thursday, marking what appears to be the first Ukrainian attack causing fatalities in the regional capital, Simferopol. Three people were killed and seven wounded there in strikes on what officials described as non-residential facilities; a separate drone strike on a commuter train near Kerch killed one more person and injured three.

The strikes come amid a broader Ukrainian offensive targeting Russian-held and Russian territory. On Wednesday, Ukraine struck an oil terminal near St. Petersburg and a naval base at Kronstadt, home of Russia's Baltic Fleet, hours before the opening of Russia's flagship St. Petersburg Economic Forum. President Zelensky confirmed Ukrainian drones had hit multiple locations across Russia.

Thursday's Crimea attacks represent the third consecutive day Ukraine has been accused of striking civilian transportation in occupied territories. Earlier in the week, a drone hit a passenger bus in Russian-controlled Donetsk, killing eight. Russia has continued its own strikes on Ukrainian cities; a mass missile and drone attack on Monday killed at least 22 people across Ukraine.

The escalating exchange of long-range strikes underscores the widening geographic scope of the conflict. Ukraine has framed its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure and naval assets as targeting the logistical backbone of Russia's war machine, while Moscow has not publicly responded to German allegations that Russia lobbied internationally against German membership on the UN Security Council partly over Berlin's support for Kyiv.

stories.headline: Armed Clashes Erupt in Mogadishu as Somalia's Political Crisis Turns Violent
stories.summary:
Heavy gunfire erupted across multiple neighborhoods of Somalia's capital, Mogadishu, on Thursday after opposition forces called for protests against President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's one-year term extension. Mohamud's constitutional term ended on May 15, and opposition leaders declared the extension illegal, triggering the standoff.

Police said they were conducting a large-scale security operation against armed militias who had launched mortar attacks in parts of the city. Former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire said he was attacked by government forces while preparing for what he described as a planned peaceful demonstration. Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed, speaking from the opposition camp, vowed the violence would not stop protests from proceeding.

The U.S. Embassy in Mogadishu condemned the violence as "reckless" and called on leaders across all sides to resolve differences through peaceful means. The number of casualties had not been confirmed as of Thursday.

The crisis marks a significant setback for Somalia's fragile democratic transition. President Mohamud had been working to replace the country's clan-based electoral system with direct elections — Somalia's first one-person, one-vote contest since 1969. The collapse of talks between the government and opposition following the term expiry has now pushed that process toward armed confrontation.

stories.headline: China Bans Four New Zealand MPs Over Taiwan Visit in Unprecedented Move
stories.summary:
China has imposed one-year travel bans on four New Zealand Members of Parliament who visited Taiwan in May, New Zealand's foreign ministry confirmed Thursday. The Chinese Embassy said the ban could be reduced or waived if the MPs apologized, calling their visit an interference in China's internal affairs that sent "wrong signals" to Taiwan's ruling Democratic Progressive Party.

New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters described the move as surprising, noting that New Zealand MPs have visited Taiwan for decades without such consequences and that such visits are consistent with New Zealand's One China policy. Peters has instructed foreign ministry officials in Beijing and Wellington to engage Chinese authorities to better understand what he called a "departure from past practice."

The four MPs targeted are Maureen Pugh, David Wilson, and Laura McClure from the ruling coalition, and Duncan Webb from the opposition Labour Party. McClure called the ban "a type of foreign interference" and said she would not apologize, asserting that New Zealand parliamentarians have the right to travel freely as part of living in a democracy.

The move represents an escalation in China's efforts to restrict Taiwan's international engagement. Beijing has previously criticized New Zealand parliamentary delegations to Taiwan but had never before imposed formal travel sanctions. The episode adds to growing tensions between Western-aligned democracies and Beijing over Taiwan contacts.

stories.headline: Germany Loses UN Security Council Bid; Foreign Minister Blames Russian Lobbying
stories.summary:
Germany failed to secure a rotating seat on the UN Security Council on Wednesday, losing to Portugal and Austria in a vote among UN member states. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul called the outcome a "bitter defeat" and said Russia had actively lobbied against Germany because of Berlin's firm backing for Ukraine. Germany received 104 votes compared to Portugal's 134 and Austria's 131.

Wadephul also suggested Germany's strong support for Israel in the Middle East conflict may have cost votes among member states that do not share that position. He acknowledged that Germany's late entry into the race was also a factor. Russia has not publicly responded to the accusations of lobbying against Germany's candidacy.

The result is a political setback for Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who took office emphasizing his intent to raise Germany's standing in international institutions. Opposition parties were quick to describe the loss as an embarrassment abroad compounding domestic difficulties at home.

The Security Council is the only UN body empowered to make legally binding decisions, including imposing sanctions and authorizing the use of force. Also elected to the council were Kyrgyzstan, Trinidad and Tobago, and Zimbabwe. Merz congratulated Portugal and Austria and said Germany would remain a "reliable pillar of the multilateral system."
